sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** No. The only picture is the full-bleed background behind the hero (y≈72–800, the whole width): hundreds of flat ovals in about a dozen greens, scattered at random angles. It isn't a fern or a shady spot in a garden. It doesn't even look like foliage; it looks like green confetti. The headline promises "Ferns and shade plants for every corner" and the picture shows neither, so it adds nothing to the words. A visitor who came to see what kind of ferns this place grows gets no plant to look at. The pattern also reads as generic filler, the kind of hero any green-themed site could use, so nothing here belongs to Fernhill in particular. Direction: replace the pattern with a real photo of the stock that shows the claim, such as a fern-filled shady corner or the greenhouse itself, and leave a calm area behind the headline. If it stays an illustration, draw recognisable fern fronds. **Taste** (the relevant entry has no approved source; the argument is that a nursery's hero should show the plants it sells). Weight: **major**.
2. **Do the colors, shapes, and directions of the piece carry the mood its message calls for?** No. The subject is shade, which suggests cool, dim and calm. The background is the opposite: high-chroma lime and grass greens (bright ovals around (1150,140), (1220,520) and (300,580)) on a mid-green ground, every shape tilted a different way. The result feels sunny, loud and restless, like a spring-sale banner, where the subject calls for a quiet woodland corner. The color's temperature and saturation work against the subject (Itten, *The Art of Color*). The random scatter of diagonals adds energy where calm is wanted (taste). Direction: lower the saturation and value, shift toward cooler, deeper greens with dappled light, and give the shapes a calmer, more settled direction. A shaded-garden photo would do all of this at once. **Convention** for the color mood, **taste** for the shapes and directions. Weight: **major** (it sets the wrong tone for a shade-plant specialist, and the same busyness is what fights the headline).

**What's working.**
- The piece states its job in one sentence. "Ferns and shade plants for every corner" plus "Grown on the hill and ready to plant this weekend" tell a first-time visitor what the place sells, that it's local, and that the stock is ready now. The second line has a real, specific hook ("this weekend").
- It holds together as one thing. One sans-serif family, white type on green, an outlined button and a plain white nav bar share a single modern, flat era and mood, with nothing extra or out of place apart from the background problem above.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (main image and headline make one idea; colors, shapes, directions carry the mood)

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands on the big white headline "Ferns and shade plants for every corner", drops to the subline, then to the outlined button. The leaf pattern is loud, and it tugs at the eye on the right half, where there's no text. It reads as the homepage hero for a small plant nursery's shop. It feels fresh, though busy.

Job (assumed): a nursery homepage hero that should tell visitors what's sold and get them to browse the stock.

The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image.

What matters first:
- One element dominates: **yes**. The headline at about 72 px bold white (x 96–645, y 265–470) is far bigger than anything else. The busy background takes some of its punch, but it is still clearly first.
- Levels distinct, no near-same sizes: **yes**. The headline (~72 px bold), subline (~22 px regular), button label (~17 px bold), logo (~21 px bold, dark green, on white bar) and nav (~15 px regular, grey) all have clear jobs. The logo and subline are close in size but sit in separate zones with different colour and weight, so they don't collide.
- Headings differ by more than size: **yes**. The headline is bold, the subline regular. The logo is bold and coloured, the nav regular grey.

No line answered no or unsure, so I didn't open any entries.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

(Outside this section's lines, for the director: the ghost button at x 96–356, y 569–627 is the lightest element in the hero stack, a thin white outline over a busy leaf field. The main action carries less visual weight than the subline above it. That belongs under interface or colour, not here.)

**What's working.**
- **The headline clearly comes first.** It's about three times the size of anything else, in heavy white, and it sits left at the top of the stack. The eye has one obvious place to start, and the line names what the shop sells.
- **The top bar is calm.** The dark-green bold logo and light grey regular nav sit on a plain white bar. That keeps wayfinding readable and clearly second, so it never competes with the hero headline.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Walk: Arrangement and space.** I couldn't run Bash, so there are no crops or entry lookups. The image is 1280×800, one screen, so I worked from the whole image.
- One grid: no. The logo sits at x≈64 and the nav ends at x≈1216 (a 64 px margin), but the hero block's left edge is at x≈96.
- Exact alignment or clearly off: yes. The headline, subline and button all share x≈96.
- Baselines across columns: yes, there is only one text column.
- Space within groups smaller than between: yes.
- Boxes hold one group: yes.
- No accidental groups: yes.
- No overlap or touching: yes.
- Margin from edge: yes.
- Empty space gathered: no. The leaf pattern fills every pixel of the hero, so there is no quiet area anywhere, including behind the text.
- Balance: yes. The texture is even, and the text block on the left is offset by the busy field on the right.
- Centering for a reason: yes, the hero is left-aligned.
- One proportion: yes. The header is a thin band and the text column is about half the width.
- Eye path: yes. Headline, then subline, then button.

---

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over in scattered small gaps?** No. The hero, from y≈72 to y≈800 across the full width, is wall-to-wall leaf pattern with the same density and contrast everywhere. Nowhere is calm, including the area behind the headline, subline and button (x≈96–645, y≈265–627). The text sits on noise, so the eye has nowhere to rest. The 18 px subline and the outlined "Browse the greenhouse" button fight the leaves for every letter. The headline survives on size, but the button looks like one more shape in the texture rather than the place to click. This is negative space used as leftover rather than chosen (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems*; Refactoring UI on giving elements room). Fix direction: make a deliberate quiet zone behind the text column. A darkened or blurred band, a solid panel, or a pattern that thins out toward the left would each work. Keep the full texture to the right half, where it can be the picture. Defect, major. (It overlaps with contrast, which the text and color critics should measure. The cause here is that the layout has no quiet area.)
2. **Do all blocks, pictures included, take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid, so column lines and gutters repeat down the page?** No. The header uses a 64 px side margin: "Fernhill Nursery" starts at x≈64 and "Visit" ends at x≈1216. The hero column starts at x≈96. The 32 px jog between the logo and the headline directly below it is too small to read as a decision and too large to miss, so the page looks as if two templates were put together. Fix direction: start the hero column on the logo's x≈64, or indent the hero by a visibly deliberate amount that the rest of the page repeats. Convention (one grid, Müller-Brockmann). Minor.

**What's working.**
- The hero's text stack shares one exact left edge at x≈96: headline, subline and the button's border. The gaps grow from about 40 px to about 50 px as the stack moves from statement to action, which keeps it reading as one group with a clear order.
- The header is a quiet white band, 72 px tall, with the logo on the left and four nav links on the right, mirrored on the same 64 px margins. It keeps navigation clearly separate from the hero.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- The hero fills the whole 800 px viewport and nothing shows below it, so I can't tell whether there is more content or whether anything hints that the page scrolls. Check in a live browser.
- I couldn't check how the x≈96 column and the pattern reflow at narrower widths.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (one grid governs the page; empty space gathered into deliberate areas)

sections.report:
The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so it needs no crops. Bash is denied here, so I worked from the whole image and the reference text quoted in the checklist.

**Walk (Text):** body text large enough: yes. Captions large enough: yes (no small labels). Paragraph face plain: yes. One type plan: yes (one sans family). Small text weight: yes. Plain-background contrast: yes (the grey nav on white looks fine). Text over texture: **no**. Line length: yes. Leading: yes. Multi-line heading tight: yes. Flush left: yes. Justified: yes (none). Rag: yes. Widows/runts: yes. Heading breaks at phrases: **no** ("every / corner"). Paragraph marks: yes. Left edge crisp: yes. Long text chunked: yes. Mixed case: yes. Emphasis: yes. Display spacing tighter: yes. Kerning: yes. Lower-case tracking: yes. Caps letterspaced: yes (none). Ligatures: yes (none). Real cuts: yes. Quotes and dashes: yes (none). Tabular figures: yes (none). Real type: yes, apparently. Nothing clipped: yes.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does text over a photo, gradient, or texture stay readable at the worst point behind it?** No. All the hero text is white set straight onto the leaf pattern, with no scrim or shadow:
   - The subhead "Grown on the hill and ready to plant this weekend." (about x 96–615, y 505–530) is only about 20 px tall and runs across pale lime and mint leaves. Around x 230–330 and x 540–610, parts of letters fade into the leaves, so the reader has to work at the one line that says what the offer is.
   - The button label "Browse the greenhouse" (x 128–324, y 597) is small bold white text over the same bright leaves. Only a thin white outline sets it apart, so the button looks like part of the pattern rather than something to press.
   - The headline (y 270–470) mostly holds up because it is so big and heavy. Its counters and edges still compete with pale leaves, for example behind "shade" and "every".

   The cause is that the pattern runs from dark olive to near-white lime. Contrast at the darkest leaves passes, but at the lightest ones it looks well under 3:1 for the large headline and under 4.5:1 for the subhead and button. WCAG 1.4.3 applies at the worst point behind the text, not on average. On top of the contrast problem, the busy edges of the leaves break up the letter shapes.

   Fix: put a dark scrim or gradient behind the text column on the left. You could also darken or quiet the pattern under the text, or give the button a solid fill. Then check the contrast at the palest leaf behind each line.

   Defect, major. It weakens the subhead and the call to action, which are the parts that do the job.
2. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries?** No. The headline breaks as "Ferns and shade / plants for every / corner". This splits "every corner" and leaves one word alone on the last line, so the headline reads as three uneven lines with a stray end. Fix: rebreak it, for example "Ferns and shade plants / for every corner", or adjust the measure so the phrases stay together. Convention (Bringhurst, on line breaks in display text). Minor.

**What's working.**
- There is one sans family on a clear scale: a large bold headline, a mid-size regular subhead, and small nav and button text. Each size has an obvious job and none of them collide.
- The headline's three lines are set tight enough to read as one block, and the text column is set flush left on a shared edge at x 96.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the button label and headline are live text. They look like it.
- Whether the pattern moves or shifts behind the text. If it is animated or randomised per load, the worst-case contrast will change.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (text over texture readable at worst point; heading breaks at phrase boundaries)

sections.report:
**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the piece hold a clear range of light and dark, so its structure still shows in grayscale?** No. The hero, from y≈72 to 800 across the full width, is a field of leaf shapes. Pale lime leaves and dark olive ones are spread evenly over a mid-green ground. The only other light value on the screen is the white type and the white button outline. In grayscale, the pale lime leaves come close to white and pass right behind the letters, for example behind "shade" at x≈440–640, y≈270–330 and behind "every" and "corner." The background has no calm area of one value for the text to sit on.
   - What the viewer sees: the 80 px headline still reads, because it is big and bold.
   - The subline "Grown on the hill and ready to plant this weekend." (x≈96–615, y≈505–530) is thin and small. Leaf edges break it up, so it takes effort to read.
   - The ghost button "Browse the greenhouse" (x≈96–355, y≈569–626) has a 1–2 px white outline and no fill. Its outline merges with the light leaves behind it, so the main action looks like more texture, not like a button.
   - Why: Albers, *Interaction of Color*, and Refactoring UI say structure should come from value. Hue alone holds nothing apart here, because every color in the hero is green. WCAG F83 says text over a background image must keep its contrast at the worst point behind the letters.
   - Fix: give the text a calm value field. Put a dark scrim or gradient over the left half of the hero, set the text on a solid panel, or darken and narrow the leaf pattern's value range so no leaf gets near the white type. Give the button a solid fill so its edge does not depend on what is behind it.
   - Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Is strong, saturated color kept to a small share of the area, with most of the area neutral or muted?** No. About 90% of the screen, everything under the white header, is saturated green, with fully vivid lime and emerald leaves scattered all over. Nothing on the page is muted except the header bar. So the eye has no resting area, and saturation cannot point to anything: the leaves are as loud as the call to action, and louder than the button. The page reads as busy wallpaper, not as a calm shop window for shade plants.
   - Why: Itten, *The Art of Color*, on contrast of saturation. Refactoring UI says large areas of full saturation tire the eye and weaken emphasis.
   - Fix: fill the big area with a dark or muted shade of the green. Turn down the saturation of most leaves, or keep the vivid ones to a smaller, quieter part of the frame, such as the right side away from the text. Keep a full-strength color for the main button.
   - Defect. Weight: major. It and finding 1 are fixed by the same move: calm the background behind the text.

**What's working.**
- The palette is one hue family: greens, plus white, a deep green logo and a gray nav. It fits a fern and shade-plant nursery and says "plants" before a word is read.
- The deep green of the "Fernhill Nursery" wordmark in the header comes from the same family as the hero. That ties the brand to the image without adding another hue.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The button's hover and focus colors matter here, because its white outline is already weak against the pattern. Check in a browser that the focus ring shows against the leaves.

**Checklist.** `Color: 9 lines, 7 yes, 2 no (strong color kept to a small share; clear range of light and dark), 0 unsure`

sections.report:
**Section.** Pictures: applies. The only picture is the full-bleed hero background (y 72–800, full width), an illustrated pattern of flat leaf-shaped ellipses in many greens over a dark green ground. The "Fernhill Nursery" wordmark at the top left (about x 64–236, y 22–48) is plain set type.

**Findings**
1. **Is any texture or pattern quiet enough that it never competes with the focal point or the text over it?** No.
   - **Where:** the leaf pattern runs at full contrast and full density right behind the headline (x 96–645, y 265–470), the subhead (x 96–615, y 505–530) and the outlined button (x 96–356, y 569–627).
   - **What the viewer meets:** lime and pale green leaves sit right next to the white letters. The headline still reads because it is large and bold. The thin subhead and the ghost button's 1 px white outline break up against the leaves and take effort to pick out. The button barely separates from the pattern, so the page's one action reads as weak.
   - **Why:** the pattern is as loud as the text. It has no quiet zone, no darkening behind the copy, and no falloff toward the text column, so it competes with the focal point instead of framing it. The rule's sources are not on the approved list, so this is common sense.
   - **Fix:** calm the pattern behind the copy. Darken it or cut its contrast and density in the left half, or give the text a solid or scrimmed panel. Keep the full pattern on the right side, where nothing sits over it. Give the button a solid fill so it does not depend on a hairline outline.
   - **Kind:** defect. **Weight:** major.
2. **Do surfaces look like what they are, with no fake bevels, textures, or depth?** No, on the "claims not supported by the image" half of the line.
   - **Where:** the whole hero.
   - **What the viewer meets:** the headline promises "Ferns and shade plants", but the picture shows generic, randomly scattered ellipses in bright, sunlit lime greens. There are no fronds, no shade and no plant you could buy. Nothing in the image shows what the nursery grows, so the claim rests on the words alone, and the hero could belong to any "green" brand.
   - **Why:** this is my judgment as a designer. The entry's source (Rams) is off the approved list. For a nursery, the picture is the strongest evidence of the product, and here it says nothing about the product.
   - **Fix:** show the product. Use a photo or illustration of real ferns and shade plants, ideally in shade, so the image proves the headline. If the pattern stays, draw it as fern fronds in deep, cool shade greens rather than generic leaves.
   - **Kind:** taste. **Weight:** major.

**What's working.** The pattern is clean, sharp vector work in one consistent flat style and one level of detail. Nothing is pixelated, stretched or mixed in style. The wordmark has generous clear space in the white header and is a plain one-colour set of type, so it holds up small.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 10 yes, 2 no (texture quiet behind text; honest surfaces / claims supported by the image), 0 unsure

**Section.** Charts and data: skipped. The image is a plant nursery's hero section (header, headline, subline, button, leaf pattern), with no charts, tables of figures or dashboards.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: skipped

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has a top nav (Plants, Pots, Care guides, Visit), a logo, and one hero button, "Browse the greenhouse".

**Findings**
1. **Is exactly one button styled as the primary action, with every other action styled lower?** and **Do input borders, control edges, and meaningful icons reach 3:1 contrast against what is next to them?** These are one problem. "Browse the greenhouse" (about x 96–356, y 569–627) is the page's only call to action, but it is styled as a secondary action. It has a thin white outline and no fill, which is the emphasis Material Design 3 and Apple HIG give to secondary buttons. Behind it is a busy field of leaf ellipses, the same light shapes found everywhere in the hero. Where the outline runs over the pale lime leaves, its edge looks to be well under 3:1 (about 1.7:1 against the lightest lime, judged by eye). The button's shape breaks up into the leaves around it, so it reads as a framed caption more than a control. The viewer's eye goes to the 72 px headline and the leaves, and the one thing they can do on the page is the weakest-looking thing in the hero.
   - **Direction:** give it the primary treatment, a solid fill such as white with dark green text, or a deep green fill with a clear edge, so it stands out from the leaves and is plainly the next step. Or calm the background behind the text column (a scrim or a darker overlay) so the edge reaches 3:1 all the way round.
   - Convention (Material 3 / HIG button emphasis; WCAG 1.4.11 non-text contrast) with a defect consequence. Weight: **major**.
2. **Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search, filters, or keyboard hints?** The header (y 0–72) has four text links and nothing else: no search and no basket or cart. The words "Browse the greenhouse" and "ready to plant this weekend" suggest people can shop here. Someone who already knows which fern they want has to browse "Plants" by hand, with no quick way to find it. NN/g's heuristic 7 (Nielsen) says to give frequent actions accelerators such as search.
   - **Direction:** if the site sells online, put a search field or icon and a basket in the top right, where Jakob's law says people look for them. If it doesn't sell online (a catalogue for an in-person visit), this finding goes away.
   - Convention. Weight: **minor**.

**What's working.**
- The nav is short, plain and conventional: logo top left, four links top right. The four labels (Plants, Pots, Care guides, Visit) use a gardener's own words and show how the site is laid out at a glance.
- The hero has only one action, so nothing competes with it. The problem is how it is styled, not how many actions there are.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus: whether the outline button and the nav links show a visible focus ring. A white button outline on leaves makes a default focus ring hard to see too.
- Whether the header is sticky and could cover focused content when scrolling.
- Hover and pressed states of the button, which matter here because the default state is so light.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 29 yes, 3 no (one button styled as primary; 3:1 contrast on control edges; shortcuts such as search), 1 unsure (focus indicator 2 px at 3:1).
